description: A fast-growing, slender deciduous tree 5-10 m tall with soft wood, feathery tripinnate leaves with small oval leaflets, fragrant creamy-white flowers and long ridged green pods (drumsticks) up to 30-45 cm.
cultural_significance: A staple of South Indian cuisine (sambar, poriyal) and the 'miracle tree' of nutrition programmes worldwide. Shigru is described in Samhitas and Nighantus. Not a Vedic-era plant by name with certainty.
habitat: Dry to humid tropics; grows in sandy loam and tolerates drought; commonly planted in backyards and farms across India.

uses.title: Nutritional support
uses.detail: Leaves and pods are eaten as vegetables rich in iron, vitamin C, vitamin A, calcium and protein, and are used against dietary deficiency.

uses.title: Joint pain and inflammation
uses.detail: Shigru is traditionally described as Shothahara and Vedanasthapana, with bark and root used in swellings and rheumatic pain.

uses.title: Digestion and worms
uses.detail: Pods and leaves are described as Deepana and Krimighna (appetiser, anti-worm).

uses.title: Eye and heart support
uses.detail: Traditionally described as Chakshushya (good for eyes) and Hridya.

uses.title: Blood sugar research
uses.detail: Leaf studies report modest effects on blood sugar and lipids; evidence is preliminary.

preparations.name: Leaf stir-fry or soup
preparations.method: Cook fresh leaves lightly with oil, spices and lentils or add to soups.

preparations.name: Pod curry (sambar)
preparations.method: Cut drumsticks into pieces and simmer in lentil sambar; scrape the pulp when eating.

preparations.name: Leaf powder
preparations.method: Shade-dry leaves and grind to powder; mix into food or smoothies.

preparations.name: Root or bark poultice
preparations.method: Crushed root or bark paste applied on swellings.

precautions: Root, root bark and bark should be avoided in pregnancy as they may stimulate the uterus; leaves in food amounts are generally eaten. May lower blood sugar and blood pressure, so people on diabetes or BP medicines should consult a doctor. Large amounts of leaf powder can cause loose stools. Allergy is possible.

cultivation.harvest: Leaves from a few months; pods 6-8 months after planting

fun_fact: A single moringa tree can grow 3-4 m in its first year from seed, and its seeds are used to clarify water in some rural communities.

regions.name: South Asia (Widely cultivated)
regions.note: Backyards and farms across the subcontinent
